quiz.title: Financial literacy quiz
quiz.intro: Try four questions on budgeting, fees, inflation and diversification.

budget.question: What do you compare to see how much money is left in a monthly budget?
budget.explanation: Subtracting monthly expenses from monthly income shows whether money is left over or spending exceeds income.

fees.question: If two investments have the same gross return, what do higher fees do to the return you keep?
fees.explanation: Fees are deducted from your investment, so a higher fee leaves you with less when the gross return is the same.

inflation.question: If prices generally rise and your income stays the same, what happens to your purchasing power?
inflation.explanation: When prices rise, the same amount of money buys fewer goods and services.

diversification.question: What is one reason to spread money across different investments?
diversification.choice0: To reduce dependence on any single investment
diversification.choice2: To make every investment move together
diversification.explanation: Diversification can reduce the impact of a single investment performing poorly. A diversified portfolio can still lose value.

mission.title: Our Mission
mission.statement: Empowering Better Lives Through Financial Clarity
mission.description: We believe that a better future begins with the right tools. Our mission is to provide families with a simple, all-in-one platform to make smarter financial decisions. By helping our users understand how they spend, save, and earn, we aim to tackle a fundamental challenge in society: the lack of financial literacy. From budgeting to investing, Wonder.Money brings everything together to give you the confidence to manage your financial journey.

story.title: Our Story
story.paragraph1: We started WonderMoney because we were frustrated. Managing personal finances in Europe meant juggling five different apps - one for each bank account, another for budgets, a spreadsheet for investments, and still never having a clear picture. The tools that existed were either built for the US market, overpriced, or too complicated for everyday use.
story.paragraph2: So we built what we wanted to use ourselves: a single, beautifully simple app that connects to your banks via Open Banking, organizes your transactions automatically, tracks your budgets, and monitors your investments. All in one place, built for Europeans, at a price that makes sense.
story.paragraph3: We're still early. WonderMoney is growing fast, shaped by feedback from real users who are part of our beta. Every week we ship new features, fix what's broken, and get closer to our vision: a world where understanding your finances is effortless. We're building this in Portugal, for Europe, and we're just getting started.

guide.exampleBudget: A {{amount}} budget in {{from}} needs {{equivalent}} in {{to}} to buy the same basket. Average prices changed by {{inflation}}.
guide.exampleInvestment: If an investment rose from {{amount}} in {{from}} to {{finalValue}} in {{to}}, the final balance would be worth {{realValue}} in {{from}} euros.
guide.method: We use the annual average of Portugal’s all-items consumer price index (CPI), with {{baseYear}} as the base year. Each year represents average prices from January to December. Divide the comparison-year CPI by the starting-year CPI, then multiply the starting amount by that ratio. Divide the final balance by the same ratio to express it in starting-year euros.
guide.limitations: Your own spending can differ from the national basket. The investment comparison assumes a single starting and final balance with zero contributions or withdrawals. It uses the nominal balance you enter, so fees and taxes are reflected only if they are already included. Enter euro amounts throughout, converting any historical escudo figures first.

guide.source: INE annual CPI via Banco de Portugal, series {{id}}

propertyTax.title: Property tax (IMI) calculator
propertyTax.subtitle: Estimate the annual IMI bill on a property in Portugal, see when each instalment falls due and how much to set aside every month.
propertyTax.description: Estimate Portuguese IMI, the instalment dates and a monthly provision.
propertyTax.pageTitle: IMI Calculator: Portuguese Property Tax and Payment Dates
propertyTax.pageDescription: Estimate your annual IMI from the taxable property value and municipal rate, see the May, August and November instalments and the monthly amount to set aside.
propertyTax.vptHelp: The VPT is on your property tax booklet (caderneta predial) and on the IMI notice.
propertyTax.rateHelp: Each municipality sets its own rate for urban property, between {{min}} and {{max}}. The default is only an example: use your municipality's rate.
propertyTax.rusticNote: Rustic property is taxed at the national rate of {{rate}}. There is no municipal rate to enter.
propertyTax.dependantsHelp: Only if the property is your permanent home and your municipality applies the IMI Familiar reduction. Many do not, or only from a given number of dependants.

errors.negative: Enter zero or a positive value.
errors.rateRange: Enter a rate from {{min}} to {{max}}, the legal range for urban property.
errors.dependants: Choose a number of dependants from the list.
errors.summary: Check the highlighted fields to see your estimate.

result.nothingDue: Nothing to pay: the reduction covers the whole bill.
result.belowMinimum: Nothing to collect: IMI below €10 is not assessed (article 113 of the Código do IMI).

guide.example: A property with a VPT of {{vpt}} in a municipality that charges {{rate}} owes {{tax}} a year. Because the bill is above €500, it is paid in three instalments of {{instalment}} in May, August and November. Setting aside {{monthly}} a month covers it.
guide.methodTax: Annual IMI is the VPT times the rate, rounded to the cent. Urban property uses the rate your municipality set, which by law lies between 0.30% and 0.45%. Rustic property uses 0.8%.
guide.methodFamily: If you choose a number of dependants, the fixed IMI Familiar amount (€30 for one, €70 for two, €140 for three or more) is subtracted from the bill, and the bill never goes below zero. Whether it applies is up to your municipality.
guide.methodPayment: The bill is paid in one instalment in May up to €100, in two in May and November from €100 up to €500, and in three in May, August and November above €500. Instalments are equal; any cent of rounding goes to the last one.
guide.methodBudget: The monthly provision divides the annual bill by 12, so the money is ready when each instalment is due.
guide.exemptionTitle: Exemption for your own permanent home
guide.exemption: Some owners of a permanent home are exempt from IMI. Article 46 of the tax benefits statute (EBF) gives {{ebfYears}} years of exemption after buying or building a home with a VPT up to {{ebfVpt}}, if the household's gross income in the previous year was at most {{ebfIncome}}. The municipal assembly can extend it by another {{ebfExtraYears}} years. You must make the home your permanent residence within six months. On a purchase the exemption is automatic; after building or improving a home you must claim it within the deadline. A household can get it only twice. Article 11-A of the Código do IMI exempts, with no time limit, a home of a household whose gross income is at most 2.3 times 14 IAS (about €17,300 with the 2026 IAS of €537.13) and whose properties have a combined VPT of at most 10 times 14 IAS (€75,198.20 at the 2026 IAS). Other conditions apply and limits can change, so the calculator does not apply any exemption. Check your eligibility on the Portal das Finanças before using the result.
guide.assumptionRate: The municipal rate is yours to enter. This page does not hold a table of municipal rates, and municipalities can also raise or lower the rate in specific cases, for example for vacant or dilapidated buildings, which the calculator ignores.
guide.assumptionScope: The estimate covers a single property taxed under the ordinary rules. It excludes additional IMI (AIMI), the temporary exemptions and any other municipal deduction.
guide.assumptionEducational: This is an educational estimate, not tax advice. The amount on your IMI notice from the Tax Authority is the one that counts.
guide.sourceRates: Código do IMI, article 112: rates (consulted 19 November 2026)
guide.sourcePayment: Código do IMI, article 120: payment in instalments (consulted 19 November 2026)
guide.sourceExemption: Código do IMI, article 11-A: low-income exemption (consulted 20 November 2026)
guide.reviewed: Rules reviewed on 20 November 2026 for the IMI payable in 2026 and 2027. The IMI Familiar amounts come from article 112-A of the Código do IMI (Portal das Finanças).
guide.methodMinimum: If the tax to collect, after any IMI Familiar reduction, is below €10, no IMI is assessed and the calculator shows €0 with a note (article 113(6) of the Código do IMI).
guide.sourceMinimum: Código do IMI, article 113: assessment, no IMI below €10 (consulted 19 November 2026)
guide.sourceEbf: Tax benefits statute (EBF), article 46: own-home exemption, in the wording of Lei n.º 82/2023, the same as the Diário da República consolidated text (consulted 20 November 2026)

fire.title: FIRE Calculator
fire.description: Work out how much you need invested to live off it, and how long your savings take to get there.
fire.annualSpendingHelp: What you expect to spend a year once you stop working, in today's money
fire.currentAssetsHelp: Funds, shares, bonds and pension savings you could live off. Leave out your home.
fire.monthlyContributionHelp: What you add to your investments each month
fire.realReturnHelp: After inflation. Use a figure between {{min}} and {{max}}.
fire.withdrawalRateHelp: The share of your investments you take out in the first year, between {{min}} and {{max}}.
fire.clampedNote: Using {{value}}, the nearest value the calculator allows.
fire.reached: You are already there: what you have invested covers your FIRE number at a {{rate}} withdrawal rate.
fire.unreachable: At these figures your investments never reach your FIRE number. Add a monthly contribution or raise the expected return to see a date.
fire.unreachableWithContribution: At these figures your investments level off below your FIRE number and never reach it. Raise your monthly contribution or the expected return to see a date.
fire.beyondHorizon: Not within {{years}} years at these figures. The chart shows the first {{years}} years; a higher contribution or lower spending brings the date closer.
fire.noSpending: Enter your annual spending to see your FIRE number.
fire.missingRate: Enter a real return and a withdrawal rate to see your FIRE number.
fire.sensitivity: Spending {{cut}} less, {{spending}} a year, lowers the target to {{target}} and gets you there in {{time}}.
fire.sensitivityReached: Spending {{cut}} less, {{spending}} a year, lowers the target to {{target}}, which your investments already cover.
fire.tableToggle: Show the projection as a table
fire.assumptions: Amounts are in today's money, because the return is after inflation. Taxes, fees and sequence risk (poor returns in the first years of withdrawals) are not included.

guide.exampleBody: Say you expect to spend {{spending}} a year once you stop working. You have {{assets}} invested, add {{contribution}} a month and expect a real return of {{return}} a year.
guide.exampleTarget: At a {{rate}} withdrawal rate, your FIRE number is {{spending}} ÷ {{rate}} = {{target}}, so today's {{assets}} is {{progress}} of the way there.
guide.exampleTime: Growing month by month with the contributions added, the investments pass {{target}} after {{time}}. Spend {{cut}} less, {{cutSpending}} a year, and the target falls to {{cutTarget}}, reached after {{cutTime}}. The calculator above starts from these figures, so you can replace them with yours.
guide.methodMultipleBody: At 4% the target is 25 times your annual spending; at 3% it is about 33 times. A lower rate gives a larger target and more room for bad years.
guide.methodGrowthBody: Each month your investments grow at the monthly rate that compounds to the annual return you enter, then that month's contribution is added. The time shown is the first month the total reaches your FIRE number.
guide.methodRealMoneyBody: The return is real, after inflation, so every figure is in today's money. Your spending and contributions are assumed to rise with prices, which is why they stay the same in the calculation.
guide.methodHorizonBody: The projection stops after {{years}} years. If contributions and growth cannot reach the target, for example with no contribution and no return, the calculator says so instead of giving a date.
guide.methodLeftOutBody: Taxes on gains and withdrawals, fund and platform fees, and sequence risk, the danger of poor returns in the first years you live off your investments. A withdrawal rate is a rule of thumb drawn from past market returns, not a guarantee.
guide.methodPrivacyBody: The calculation runs in your browser. The figures you enter stay on your device and are not saved.

formula.assetsEnd: Investments at the end of the month

compoundInterest.inflationHelp: Used to show the result in today's money. The European Central Bank targets 2% a year.
compoundInterest.summary: After {{years}}, the {{contributed}} you pay in grows to {{final}}. In today's money that is worth {{real}}.
compoundInterest.statusNothingInvested: Enter an initial amount or a monthly contribution to see it grow.

compoundInterest.inflationWarning: Inflation is at or above the expected return, so this money barely keeps or loses its purchasing power. Growth after inflation: {{growth}}.
compoundInterest.adjusted: Some values were outside the accepted range and were adjusted: amounts from 0 to {{maxAmount}}, return and inflation from 0% to {{maxRate}}%, and 0 to {{maxYears}} years.
compoundInterest.assumptions: Assumes a constant return, contributions at the end of each month and no taxes or fees.
compoundInterest.chartLabel: Chart of the projected value by year: amount paid in, growth and value in today's money. The same figures are in the table by year.
compoundInterest.tableCaption: Projected value at the end of each year

guide.whatBody1: Compound interest is growth on top of growth. When the return on your money stays invested, it starts earning a return of its own, so each year's growth is a little larger than the year before.
guide.whatBody2: Early on, most of the balance is what you paid in. Over long periods the growth can overtake it. That is why the number of years matters as much as the rate, and why starting earlier usually beats paying in more later.
guide.realHeading: Nominal value and value in today's money
guide.realBody1: The nominal value is the number of euros you would have at the end. Prices rise in the meantime, so those euros buy less than the same euros today.
guide.realBody2: The value in today's money divides that result by the inflation built up over the period. It answers a more useful question: what the final amount would buy if you had it now. The calculator shows both side by side.
guide.exampleIntro: You start with {{principal}}, pay in {{monthly}} a month for {{years}} years and expect a {{rate}} return a year, with {{inflation}} inflation a year. These are the calculator's starting values.
guide.exampleStep1: Paid in: {{principal}} at the start plus {{monthly}} × {{months}} months = {{contributed}}.
guide.exampleStep2: Growth: {{growth}}, so the final value is {{final}}. The growth ends up larger than everything you paid in.
guide.exampleStep3: In today's money the final value is {{realFinal}}: what you paid in is worth {{realContributed}} and the growth after inflation is {{realGrowth}}.
guide.exampleComparison: Raising the contribution to {{comparisonMonthly}} a month adds {{extraContributed}} paid in over the period and {{extraFinal}} to the final value, which reaches {{comparisonFinal}}. In today's money the difference is {{extraReal}}.
guide.methodMonthlyBody: The annual return is split into 12 equal monthly rates. Each month the balance grows by that rate, then the contribution is added at the end of the month. A {{rate}} return compounded monthly gives {{effectiveRate}} over a full year.
guide.methodInflationBody: Inflation is converted to an equivalent monthly rate that compounds to the annual rate. The final value is divided by the inflation built up over the whole period, and each contribution by the inflation built up until the month it is paid, so the amount paid in is shown in today's money too.
guide.methodRoundingBody: Growth is rounded to the cent every month. Totals are shown in whole euros, and growth is always the final value minus what was paid in, so the figures add up.
guide.methodRangesBody: Amounts go from 0 to {{maxAmount}}, return and inflation from 0% to {{maxRate}}%, and the period from 0 to {{maxYears}} whole years. Values outside these ranges are adjusted, and the calculator tells you when that happens.
guide.methodPrivacyBody: The calculation runs in your browser. The amounts you enter are not sent anywhere.
guide.assumption1: The return is the same every year.
guide.assumption2: Contributions go in at the end of each month and stay the same throughout.
guide.assumption3: No taxes, fees or commissions are taken off.
guide.assumption4: Inflation is the same every year.
guide.assumptionsNote: Real investments move up and down, and taxes and fees lower what you keep. Treat the result as a projection to compare options, not a forecast.
guide.rateBody1: Use the return you expect after costs and before inflation. A savings account or government bonds return less than a diversified stock fund, which can grow more over long periods but also loses value in some years.
guide.rateBody2: If you are unsure, try a cautious rate and a more optimistic one and compare the results. The gap between them shows how much of the outcome depends on the rate, which you do not control, and how much on the contribution and the period, which you do.

investorProfile.methodHeading: How the quiz scores your answers
investorProfile.dimensions: The first three answers describe your financial capacity: when you need the money, how flexible that date is and whether you have a separate cash buffer. The other three describe your comfort with risk: your reaction to a drop, how you feel about fluctuations and your preference between stability and growth potential.
investorProfile.method: Each answer earns 0, 1 or 2 points in the order shown. Each group adds up to 0–6 points. The lower of the two scores sets your result: 0–2 is lower, 3–4 is moderate and 5–6 is higher.
investorProfile.example: If your first three answers score 0, 1 and 1, your capacity is 2 out of 6. If the other three score 2 each, your comfort is 6 out of 6. The result is the lower band because capacity is the smaller score.
investorProfile.limitations: The quiz uses hypothetical scenarios and your own estimates for one goal. Your answers may change with your finances or the goal. The scoring is a teaching heuristic and has not been validated as a suitability assessment. It provides no investment advice.

emergencyFund.currentSavingsHelp: Cash you have already set aside and can reach quickly
emergencyFund.monthlyContributionHelp: What you can set aside for this fund each month
emergencyFund.statusNoExpenses: Enter your essential monthly expenses to see your target.
emergencyFund.statusReached: Your savings already cover {{months}} of essential expenses.
emergencyFund.statusNoContribution: Without a monthly contribution the fund stays at {{savings}} and never reaches the target. Add an amount you can set aside each month.
emergencyFund.statusOnTrack: Setting aside {{contribution}} a month closes the {{shortfall}} gap in {{months}}.
emergencyFund.statusBeyondHorizon: At {{contribution}} a month it would take more than 100 years to reach the target. Try a larger contribution or fewer months of cover.
emergencyFund.noInterest: This calculation does not add interest to your savings.
emergencyFund.guidanceRange: A common rule of thumb is 3 to 6 months of essential expenses: {{low}} to {{high}} for you.
emergencyFund.guidanceRangeGeneric: A common rule of thumb is 3 to 6 months of essential expenses.
emergencyFund.guidanceHigher: Aim higher, towards 9 to 12 months, if your income is irregular (freelance, commission or seasonal work), you are the only earner in your household, or children or other people depend on you.
emergencyFund.whatTitle: What an emergency fund is for
emergencyFund.whatBody1: An emergency fund is cash kept aside for the things you cannot plan: losing your job, an urgent repair, a medical bill. It lets you pay for them without a credit card balance or a personal loan, and without selling investments at a bad moment.
emergencyFund.whatBody2: Size it on essential expenses only, the costs that keep going if your income stops: housing, food, utilities, transport, insurance and minimum loan payments. Leave out spending you could pause. Keep the money somewhere safe that you can withdraw from quickly and without a penalty, such as a savings account, rather than invested.
emergencyFund.exampleIntro: Say your essential costs come to {{expenses}} a month, you already have {{savings}} set aside and you can save {{contribution}} a month. You choose {{months}} months of cover.
emergencyFund.exampleOutro: With 3 months of cover instead, the target is {{lowTarget}} and you reach it in {{lowMonths}} months. Start smaller if a long goal is putting you off, then raise the target once the first months are covered.
emergencyFund.method1: Target = essential monthly expenses × months of cover.
emergencyFund.method2: Still to save = target − emergency savings today. When your savings are higher, the difference is shown as the amount above your target.
emergencyFund.method3: Time to reach it = still to save ÷ monthly contribution, rounded up to a whole month. The target month counts that many months from this one, with one contribution a month starting next month.
emergencyFund.method4: Your savings earn no interest here, and your expenses and contribution stay the same every month. Interest would get you there a little sooner and rising prices a little later, so check the numbers again once or twice a year.
emergencyFund.nextStepHeadline: Create and track your emergency-fund goal
emergencyFund.nextStepDescription: Save this target as a goal in WonderMoney and follow your progress against your real account balances.

guide.whatHeading: What the debt-to-income ratio tells you
guide.whatBody: The debt-to-income ratio is the share of a household's take-home pay that is already promised to credit each month. Lenders use it to judge whether a new loan fits, and it is a quick check on how much room the budget has once every instalment is paid.
guide.bandHealthyBody: Repayments leave most of the income for living costs, savings and the unexpected.
guide.bandCautionBody: Repayments take a large share. The budget still works, but a drop in income or a higher rate on a variable loan would be felt.
guide.bandHighBody: Repayments take a heavy share. Many lenders would hesitate to add credit, and there is little slack left for anything else.
guide.limitsBody: These bands are a general guide, not a legal rule. Lenders and regulators set their own limits, they vary by country, and they may count income or payments differently, for example by testing the payment at a higher interest rate. Ask your lender which limit and definitions apply to you.
guide.exampleBody: A couple brings home {{income}} a month between them. They pay {{home}} on their mortgage, {{car}} on a car loan and {{cards}} towards a credit card, {{total}} in all. Divide the payments by the income and multiply by 100: their ratio is {{ratio}}, in the caution band.
guide.exampleScenario: Their car loan ends soon. Without it, payments fall to {{scenarioTotal}} and the ratio to {{scenarioRatio}}, back in the healthy band. The calculator above starts from this household and this change, so you can swap in your own figures.
guide.methodRounding: The ratio is rounded to one decimal place, and the band follows the rounded figure. Payments above income give a ratio over 100%.
guide.methodPrivacy: The calculation runs in your browser. The figures you enter stay on your device and are not saved.
guide.nextBody: A mortgage or another loan adds a payment. Work out what a new mortgage would cost each month, then enter that payment in the scenario panel to see the new ratio.
guide.methodCountsBody: Every instalment due each month on home loans, personal and car loans, credit cards, leasing and any other credit. For a card, use the amount you actually pay each month.
guide.methodExcludesBody: Rent to a landlord, bills, groceries, insurance and savings. They matter to the budget but are not repayments of borrowed money.
guide.methodIncomeBody: What reaches your account after tax and social contributions, for everyone in the household who shares the repayments. If income varies, use a monthly average over the past year.

guide.whatBody: A household budget puts a month's income next to a month's spending. Grouping the spending into a few categories turns a long list of payments into a short answer: how much is left at the end of the month, and which parts of life take the biggest slice.
guide.readSurplusBody: Income minus expenses, when it is positive. It is the money you can save, invest or set aside for bills that don't arrive every month.
guide.readDeficitBody: Expenses above income. A month like this is paid for from savings or with credit, so it is worth finding where to cut before it happens again.
guide.readSharesBody: Each category as a percentage of total income. It makes budgets of different sizes comparable and shows which category to look at first.
guide.readDiagramBody: Draws the same figures. Each band is as wide as its amount, from income on the left to the categories and the surplus on the right.
guide.exampleBody: A household earns {{salary}} in salary and {{other}} from other sources, {{income}} a month. Its expenses add up to {{expenses}}, which leaves a surplus of {{surplus}}. Divide the surplus by the income and multiply by 100: the savings rate is {{savingsRate}}.
guide.exampleFlowCaption: This household's month, from income to surplus
guide.exampleShares: Housing is the largest category at {{housing}}, or {{housingShare}} of income, followed by food at {{food}} ({{foodShare}}). Utilities combine two rows, energy and telecoms, for {{utilities}}. The calculator above starts from this household, so you can swap in your own figures.
guide.exampleSharesCaption: Each category and the surplus as a share of income
guide.methodIncomeBody: Income is net: what reaches the household's accounts after tax and social contributions. If it varies, use the monthly average of the past year.
guide.methodExpensesBody: Expenses are what leaves those accounts each month, loan repayments included. Money you move into savings is not an expense: it is part of the surplus.
guide.methodIrregularBody: For yearly or occasional costs, such as insurance, car servicing or holidays, divide the yearly amount by 12 and add it as a row.
guide.methodSharesBody: Every share is worked out on income, not on spending. With a surplus, the categories and the surplus add up to 100%; with a deficit, the categories go above 100%. Without income there are no shares and no savings rate.
guide.methodRoundingBody: Amounts are added to the cent and percentages are rounded to one decimal place. Empty and negative amounts count as zero.
guide.methodPrivacyBody: The calculation runs in your browser. The figures you enter stay on your device and are not saved or sent anywhere.
guide.nextHeading: From a one-off budget to a monthly habit
guide.nextBody: A budget is most useful when you compare it with what you actually spent. WonderMoney's envelope budgets apply the same idea month after month.
guide.nextLink: See how budgeting works in WonderMoney

example.title: Worked example
example.setup: Say you borrow {{amount}} over {{years}} years at a fixed {{rate}} a year. The monthly rate is {{rate}} divided by 12, about {{monthlyRate}}, and you make {{payments}} payments.
example.firstMonth: The level payment that clears the loan is {{payment}} a month. In the first month, interest on the full balance comes to {{firstInterest}}, so only {{firstPrincipal}} of that payment reduces what you owe.
example.total: Over the whole term you pay {{totalInterest}} in interest, {{totalPaid}} in all.

method.title: How the payment is calculated
method.intro: Most fixed-rate mortgages are repaid in level payments: the same amount every month, set so the balance reaches zero with the last one. The payment comes from the annuity formula:
method.schedule: Each month, interest is charged on the balance still owed and the rest of the payment repays principal. As the balance falls, the interest part shrinks and the principal part grows, which is why the balance falls slowly at first and faster towards the end. Insurance and fees are added on top of the payment and never reduce the balance.

assumptions.fixedRate: The rate stays the same for the whole term.
assumptions.monthly: You pay once a month, starting one month after the loan begins, with no early repayments or payment breaks.
assumptions.nominalRate: The rate you enter is a nominal annual rate. The APR a lender quotes includes fees and charges, so it is higher than the rate used here.
assumptions.flatFees: Insurance and fees are the same amount every month.
assumptions.rounding: Amounts are in euros. Each month's payment is worked out from the balance still owed and the months left, then rounded to the cent, so a payment can differ from the others by a cent and the last one clears the balance exactly. On a very long loan at a high rate, the first payments may repay less than a cent of the loan.
assumptions.lenderFigures: Your lender's figures can differ slightly, because of how they count days, round amounts or set the payment date. The pre-contract information they give you is the figure to rely on.

method.limits: The calculator accepts loans from {{minAmount}} to {{maxAmount}}, terms up to {{maxYears}} years and rates up to {{maxRate}}.
method.zeroRate: At 0% interest there is nothing to discount, so the payment is simply the loan amount divided by the number of payments.

choice.intro: When you pay off part of a loan early, the balance falls and the lender applies the cut in one of two ways. You can usually choose:
choice.lowerPaymentTitle: Keep the term and lower the payment.
choice.lowerPayment: The months left stay the same and each payment falls, which leaves you more room every month.
choice.shorterTermTitle: Keep the payment and shorten the term.
choice.shorterTerm: You keep paying the same amount and the loan ends sooner. This saves more interest, because the balance falls faster.
choice.outro: Either way you pay less interest, because from now on it is charged on a smaller balance.

fee.body: A lender may charge a percentage of the amount you repay early, and the rules and legal caps differ by country and by type of loan. Enter it in the calculator to see the net saving.

rate.term: Variable and mixed rates are out of scope
rate.body: The figures assume the rate you enter stays fixed for the rest of the loan.

reserves.body: Money paid to the lender is hard to get back, so make sure your emergency fund is still there after the repayment.

otherDebts.term: Repay the most expensive debt first
otherDebts.body: If you have a credit card or a personal loan at a higher rate, repaying it usually saves more than repaying a cheaper mortgage.

lender.term: Ask your lender how it applies the repayment
lender.body: Some lower the payment by default, others shorten the term, and many let you choose.

example.title: Worked example
example.setup: Say you still owe {{balance}} with {{term}} left at a fixed {{rate}}. You pay {{payment}} a month and, if nothing changes, the rest of the loan costs {{interest}} in interest. You repay {{repayment}} now, which leaves {{balanceAfter}} to pay.
example.lowerPayment: Keep the term and the payment falls to {{newPayment}}, {{paymentDrop}} less each month. Over the remaining {{term}} you pay {{lowerSaved}} less in interest.
example.shorterTerm: Keep paying {{payment}} and the loan ends {{timeSaved}} sooner, in {{newTerm}}, with a final payment of {{lastPayment}}. That saves {{shorterSaved}} in interest, more than lowering the payment, because the balance falls faster from the start.
example.fee: If your lender charges a {{feeRate}} fee, the repayment costs {{fee}}. The net saving is then {{lowerNet}} with the lower payment and {{shorterNet}} with the shorter term.

method.title: How it is calculated
method.intro: The calculator first works out the loan as it stands, with the same fixed-rate engine as the mortgage calculator. Each month, interest is charged on the balance still owed and the rest of the payment repays the loan. The level payment comes from the annuity formula:
method.fee: The fee is the percentage you enter, applied to the amount repaid. Interest saved is the interest left on the loan as it is minus the interest in each outcome, and the net saving is that minus the fee. A repayment larger than the balance clears the loan, and only the balance counts towards the fee.

assumptions.fixedRate: The rate stays fixed for the rest of the loan. Variable and mixed rates are not covered.
assumptions.timing: You repay the lump sum today, straight after a regular payment, and the next payment is due in a month.
assumptions.oneOff: There is one repayment, with no further extra payments or payment breaks.
assumptions.costs: Only the early repayment fee is counted. Insurance, account charges and any tax on the fee are left out.
assumptions.rounding: Amounts are in euros. Each month's interest and payment are rounded to the cent, so every total on the page adds up exactly.
assumptions.lenderFigures: Your lender's figures can differ slightly because of how it counts days and rounds. Ask for its own simulation before you repay.

method.limits: The calculator accepts balances from {{minBalance}} to {{maxBalance}}, up to {{maxYears}} years left, rates up to {{maxRate}} and fees up to {{maxFee}} of the amount repaid.
method.lowerPaymentBody: The balance left after the repayment goes back into the formula with the same number of payments, which gives the new, lower payment.
method.shorterTermBody: You go on paying what the original schedule asks for each month until the smaller balance is gone. The final payment covers only what is left, so it is usually smaller.
method.zeroRate: At 0% there is no interest, so the payment is simply the balance divided by the number of payments.

compare.title: What to compare before you switch
compare.intro: Moving your mortgage to another lender, or onto new terms with your own, can lower what you pay. A lower rate is only part of the picture, so compare the whole offer:

rate.body: A lower fixed rate cuts the interest charged on what you owe every month.

monthlyCosts.body: Lenders often ask you to take their life or home insurance, or to open an account with fees. Add them to the payment, or a cheaper rate can turn out dearer.

term.body: A new loan over more years lowers the payment, but you pay interest for longer.

oneOff.body: Leaving one loan and taking out another has fees, and they come out of your savings.

compare.outro: The calculator puts these together: the payment with its extras, the total each loan still costs and the month the switching costs are paid back.

costs.title: The costs of switching
costs.intro: What a switch costs depends on your country, your contract and the lenders involved. The usual items are:

items.exitFee: An exit or early repayment fee, a percentage of the balance your current lender charges when the loan is repaid before the end. Many countries cap it by law, and some loans have none.
items.newLoanFees: Fees for the new loan: arrangement, processing or broker fees.
items.valuation: A valuation of the home, which the new lender usually asks for.
items.legal: Legal and registration costs: notary, land registry, cancelling the old charge on the home and registering the new one, and any tax on the new loan.

costs.outro: Some lenders pay part of these costs to win your loan. Enter only what you would pay yourself, and ask each lender for the figures in writing.

example.title: Worked example
example.setup: Say you still owe {{balance}} with {{term}} left at a fixed {{currentRate}}, and pay {{currentFees}} a month in insurance and fees. Your payment is {{currentMonthly}} a month. Another lender offers {{newRate}} over the same term, with {{newFees}} a month of insurance: {{offerMonthly}} a month, {{monthlySaving}} less.
example.costs: Switching costs {{costs}}: a {{exitFeeRate}} exit fee of {{exitFee}}, {{newLoanFees}} of new loan fees, {{valuationFee}} for the valuation and {{legalFees}} of legal and registration costs. At {{monthlySaving}} a month, the switch pays for itself in month {{breakEvenMonth}}, after {{breakEvenTime}}.
example.total: Over the rest of the term, the current loan costs {{currentTotal}} in payments, insurance and fees. The new loan costs {{offerTotal}}, switching costs included. The net saving is {{netSaving}}.
example.longer: Now say the new lender offers to spread the loan over {{longerTerm}}. The payment falls to {{longerMonthly}}, {{longerSaving}} less than today, and the costs are covered sooner. But the longer term adds {{extraInterest}} in interest, and overall the switch costs {{longerNetCost}} more than keeping your current loan. A lower payment is not the same as a cheaper loan.

method.title: How it is calculated
method.intro: The calculator works out both loans with the same fixed-rate engine as the mortgage calculator, on the balance you still owe. Each month, interest is charged on the balance still owed and the rest of the payment repays the loan. The level payment comes from the annuity formula:
method.saving: A month's saving is what the current loan would cost that month minus what the new one costs. Once a loan is paid off it costs nothing, so with a longer new term the months after your current loan would have ended count as a cost. The total cost of each option is its payments, insurance and fees, plus the switching costs for the new loan. The net saving is the difference.
method.breakEven: The break-even month is the first month in which the savings so far are at least the switching costs. If that never happens before both loans end, the switch does not pay for itself.
method.longerTerm: When the new term is longer than the time left, the calculator also works out the offer over the time left, so you can see how much of the lower payment comes from the rate and how much from paying for longer.

assumptions.fixedRate: Both rates stay fixed to the end of each loan. Variable and mixed rates, and fixed periods that end in a variable rate, are not covered.
assumptions.sameBalance: The new loan takes over exactly the balance you owe today. Nothing is borrowed on top, and the switching costs are paid in cash rather than added to the loan.
assumptions.timing: The switch happens today, straight after a regular payment, and the first payment on the new loan is due in a month.
assumptions.fees: Insurance and fees stay the same each month for as long as each loan runs.
assumptions.noDiscounting: A euro saved in ten years counts the same as a euro today: there is no inflation or return on the money you save.
assumptions.rounding: Amounts are in euros. Each month's interest and payment are rounded to the cent, so every total on the page adds up exactly. The payment shown is the first one; later ones stay within a cent of it.
assumptions.lenderFigures: Lenders count days and round in their own ways, so their figures can differ slightly. Ask each one for its official offer before you decide.

method.limits: The calculator accepts balances from {{minBalance}} to {{maxBalance}}, terms up to {{maxYears}} years, rates up to {{maxRate}} and exit fees up to {{maxExitFee}} of the balance.
method.zeroRate: At 0% there is no interest, so the payment is simply the balance divided by the number of payments.

guide.whatTitle: Three ways to plan a savings goal
guide.whatBody1: Pick what you want to work out. Know the goal and the date? See how much to put aside each month. Know what you can save? See how long the goal will take. No figure in mind yet? See what you could build up over a period you choose.
guide.whatBody2: Every answer shows how much comes out of your own pocket and how much comes from growth, with a year-by-year schedule, so you can see which part of the goal is your own money.

guide.exampleIntro: Say you want {{goal}} in {{years}} years ({{months}} months). You have already saved {{savings}} and expect a return of {{rate}} a year.
guide.exampleStep2: Left alone, your {{savings}} grows to {{savingsAlone}} over {{months}} months, so your contributions and their growth have to cover the remaining {{gap}}.
guide.exampleStep3: The smallest monthly contribution that gets there is {{contribution}}. Over {{months}} months you pay in {{contributions}} and growth adds {{growth}}, for {{final}} at the end.

guide.methodIntro: Your balance grows once a month and your contribution is added at the end of each month. After n months it comes to:
guide.methodLegend: S is what you have already saved, C the monthly contribution, r the monthly rate and n the number of months. With a 0% return there is nothing to divide by r, and the balance is simply S + C × n.
guide.methodRate: The monthly rate r is the one that compounds to your annual return over twelve months: (1 + annual return)^(1/12) − 1. Dividing the annual return by 12 would overstate it slightly.
guide.methodOrder: Each month's growth is rounded to the cent before the contribution is added, so the year-by-year schedule adds up to the totals exactly.
guide.methodContribution: The contribution needed comes from solving the formula for C. It is rounded up to the cent and checked month by month, so it really does reach the goal.
guide.methodTime: The time needed is the first whole month in which the balance reaches the goal, searched up to {{maxYears}} years.
guide.assumptionReturn: The return is the same every year. Real returns vary, and investments can lose value.
guide.assumptionCosts: No taxes, fees or other charges are taken from the growth.
guide.assumptionInflation: No inflation: the goal is in euros of the day you reach it, which buy less than the same amount does today.
guide.assumptionLimits: Amounts up to {{maxAmount}}, returns from 0% to {{maxReturn}} a year and periods of up to {{maxYears}} years.

guide.whatTitle: Two limits decide how much you can borrow
guide.whatBody1: The first is monthly. Lenders want all your credit payments together to stay under a share of your net income. Take that share, subtract what you already pay on other credit, and what is left is the most the new loan's payment can be. At a given rate and term, that payment repays a loan of a set size: the most your income supports.
guide.whatBody2: The second is cash. Lenders rarely finance the whole price. The part they don't lend is your down payment, and buying also has one-off costs such as taxes, notary and registration fees. Both come out of savings, so your savings put their own ceiling on the price.
guide.whatBody3: The price within reach is the lower of the two. The calculator shows which one holds you back and how much more income or savings would lift it.
guide.relatedMortgage: works out the monthly payment, interest and year-by-year schedule of a loan you already have in mind.
guide.relatedDebtToIncome: shows what share of your income your current payments take, with the same bands this tool uses.
guide.exampleIntro: A couple brings home {{income}} a month and pays {{existing}} a month on a car loan. They have {{savings}} saved for a home, expect a fixed rate of {{rate}} over {{years}} years and plan for purchase costs of {{costsRate}} of the price. Their lender lends up to {{ltv}} of the price, and they allow {{share}} of their income for credit.
guide.exampleStep4: The lower of the two is {{monthlyPrice}}, so the monthly budget sets the limit.
guide.exampleResult: At {{price}} they would borrow {{loan}}, pay {{downPayment}} down and {{purchaseCosts}} in costs, using all of their {{savings}}. The mortgage calculator puts the payment at {{payment}} a month.
guide.exampleLift: About {{extraIncome}} more net income a month would take them to {{liftPrice}}, where the savings limit takes over.
guide.exampleSavings: With only {{lowSavings}} saved, the picture flips: the savings cover a price of {{lowSavingsPrice}}, with a loan of {{lowSavingsLoan}}, well within what their income could carry. Saving more, not earning more, is what would raise their limit. The calculator above starts from the first couple, so you can swap in your own figures.
guide.methodIntro: The calculation works out each limit on its own, then takes the lower price.
guide.methodShare: The starting share of {{share}} sits in the caution band of the debt-to-income calculator ({{caution}}% to {{high}}%). It is a rule of thumb, not a legal limit.
guide.methodCosts: At the highest price every euro of savings goes into the purchase: the costs first, the rest as the down payment. The loan covers what is left, and never more than the loan-to-value allows.
guide.methodRounding: Amounts are worked in cents. The loan is rounded down to the cent, so its first payment, worked out by the mortgage calculator, fits your room; later ones can differ by a cent. The price is exactly the loan plus the down payment, and the extra income or savings is rounded up to the euro.
guide.methodPrivacy: The calculation runs in your browser. The figures you enter stay on your device and are not saved.
guide.assumptionFixedRate: A fixed rate for the whole term, with equal monthly payments of principal and interest.
guide.assumptionSavings: All of the savings you enter go into the purchase. Keep your emergency fund out of the figure.
guide.assumptionPayment: The payment leaves out insurance, account fees and the running costs of the home, such as property tax, upkeep and utilities.
guide.assumptionCostsShare: Purchase costs are a flat share of the price. In practice taxes are often tiered and some fees are fixed amounts.
guide.lendersTitle: What lenders check that this tool doesn't
guide.lendersIntro: A lender's answer can be lower than this estimate, sometimes by a lot. Rules differ by lender and by country, and this calculator builds none of them in.

guide.whatBody: A term deposit locks an amount away with a bank for a set number of months at a fixed rate. What you earn depends on three things besides the rate: how long the money stays, whether the interest comes at the end or along the way, and how much tax is withheld from it. This calculator works through all three with the rate you enter, so you can compare offers on the same basis.

read.grossBody: Everything the deposit earns before tax.
read.taxBody: The part of each interest payment kept back for tax at the rate you enter.
read.netBody: What reaches you, gross interest minus tax.
read.finalTerm: Balance at maturity, or total received when interest is paid out
read.finalBody: The amount deposited plus all the net interest.
read.yieldBody: The net return expressed as a yearly rate, so deposits of different lengths and payment schedules can be compared side by side.

guide.exampleSetup: Say you deposit {{amount}} for {{months}} months at a gross rate of {{rate}} a year, with the interest paid at maturity. The interest is simple: the amount times the rate times the share of a year the money stays.
guide.exampleCompounded: If the same deposit pays interest every quarter and adds it to the balance, it makes {{compoundedPayments}} payments and each one earns on a slightly larger amount. Gross interest comes to {{compoundedGross}}, {{compoundedExtra}} more, for a balance of {{compoundedFinal}} and a yield of {{compoundedYield}} a year, against {{yield}} when everything is paid at the end.
guide.exampleTax: Now suppose {{taxRate}} is withheld from the interest paid at maturity, a rate chosen only as an illustration, not taken from any country's rules: the calculator starts at 0% so you can enter your own. The bank keeps {{tax}}, you receive {{net}} and you end with {{taxedFinal}}, a net yield of {{taxedYield}} a year.
guide.methodIntro: Interest is counted in whole months, without a day count. The rate you enter is a nominal annual rate: each period earns the rate times its months divided by 12.

method.maturityBody: Paid at maturity, interest is simple: one payment of the amount × rate × term in months ÷ 12.
method.periodicBody: Paid monthly, quarterly or yearly, each payment comes at the end of its period. When the term is not a whole number of periods, the last period is shorter and its interest is paid pro rata at maturity. A term shorter than one period gets a single payment at maturity.
method.reinvestBody: Interest added to the deposit is added after tax, so the deposit compounds at the payment frequency. Interest paid out leaves the deposit, so later interest is worked out on the amount deposited.
method.taxBody: Tax is taken from each payment separately and rounded to the cent, as a bank withholds it. All amounts are worked in cents, so the payment rows add up to the totals.
method.yieldBody: The net annual yield is the internal rate of return of the deposit: the yearly rate at which the amount you put in grows into everything you get back, counting each net payment in the month it is paid. Interest paid along the way therefore counts for more than the same interest at maturity. A deposit shorter than a year is assumed to be renewed on the same terms.
method.excludedBody: Early withdrawal penalties, account fees, rate changes during the term, deposit guarantee limits and the effect of inflation.
method.privacyBody: The calculation runs in your browser. The figures you enter stay on your device and are not saved or sent anywhere.

guide.whatBody: Buying swaps rent for mortgage payments, but it also ties up cash in the down payment and purchase costs and adds the costs of owning. Renting leaves that cash free to invest. The calculator follows both paths from the same starting cash and compares what each one leaves you with.

netWorth.body: For buying, what selling the home would leave after selling costs and repaying the loan, plus anything invested; for renting, the investments.

difference.body: How far ahead one path is at the end of the period you chose.

breakEven.body: The first year that ends with buying ahead. Buying starts behind whenever there are purchase or selling costs: the purchase costs are spent on day one, and selling straight away would cost the selling costs on top. Buying can also pull ahead and fall behind again, for example when the home's value grows more slowly than the renter's investments.

chart.body: The chart and the table show both paths every year, so you can see whether the gap is closing or widening.

example.setup: A home costs {{price}}. You put down {{downPayment}} ({{downPaymentShare}}) and borrow {{loan}} at {{rate}} over {{term}} years. Purchase costs of {{purchaseCostsPct}} add {{purchaseCosts}}, so buying takes {{upfront}} of cash. The same home rents for {{rent}} a month. The rest are the calculator's starting assumptions: rent up {{rentIncrease}} a year, the home's value up {{appreciation}} a year, ownership costs of {{ownershipCostsPct}} of the value a year, a {{investmentReturn}} return on investments and {{sellingCostsPct}} selling costs, over {{horizon}} years.
example.start: On day one the renter invests the {{upfront}}. The owner's stake is the {{downPayment}} down payment less {{startSellingCosts}} of selling costs, {{startOwner}}, so buying starts {{startGap}} behind.
example.monthly: In the first month owning costs {{owningMonthly}}: {{mortgagePayment}} of mortgage payment and {{ownershipMonthly}} of ownership costs. The rent is {{rentMonthly}}, so the renter invests the {{monthlyGap}} difference. In this example owning costs more than renting in every month of the {{horizon}} years, so the owner never has money left over to invest.
example.result: After {{horizon}} years the home is worth {{homeValue}}. Selling it costs {{sellingCosts}} and repays the {{loanBalance}} still owed, which leaves the owner {{ownerNetWorth}}. The renter's investments have grown to {{renterNetWorth}}, so buying ends {{difference}} ahead.
example.breakEven: Buying first pulls ahead at the end of year {{breakEvenYear}}. The answer depends on the assumptions: at a rent of {{altRent}} a month instead, renting is still {{altDifference}} ahead after {{horizon}} years.

guide.methodIntro: The calculator works month by month, in cents, from the day of purchase.

method.start: Both paths start with the same cash: the down payment plus the purchase costs. The owner spends it on the home; the renter invests all of it.
method.loan: The mortgage is the one the mortgage calculator works out: a fixed rate, with each month's payment set from the balance still owed. Payments stop once the loan is repaid.
method.monthly: Each month the owner pays the mortgage and a twelfth of the year's ownership costs, and the renter pays the rent. Whichever path costs less that month invests the difference.
method.growth: The home's value changes once a year by the growth rate. Ownership costs are a percentage of the value at the start of each year, so they change with it. The rent rises once a year by the rent increase.
method.returns: Investments grow each month at the monthly rate that compounds to the annual return over a year.
method.netWorth: At the end of each year the owner's net worth is the home's value less selling costs and the loan still owed, plus their investments. The renter's is their investments. The break-even year is the first year that ends with the owner ahead.

leftOut.gainsTax: Tax on investment gains or on the profit from selling the home.
leftOut.deposit: A rent deposit, and anything it could earn.

leftOut.budget: Whether the payments are affordable: both paths assume the higher of the two costs is paid from income every month.

guide.whatTitle: How a rate revision changes your payment
guide.whatBody1: On a variable-rate loan the rate you pay has two parts: a reference index and a spread. The index is a market or central bank rate, such as Euribor in much of the euro area, and other countries use their own. The spread is the lender's margin and is fixed in your contract.
guide.whatBody2: At each reset date, often every 3, 6 or 12 months, the lender takes the latest value of the index, adds the spread and works out a new payment on the balance and the time left. With the same spread, a rise of 1 percentage point in the index raises the rate by up to 1 percentage point, depending on any cap or floor.
guide.whatBody3: This calculator shows the payment before and after a change you choose, so you can see ahead of time what a rise or a fall would mean for your monthly budget.
guide.relatedMortgage: the full year-by-year schedule of a loan at one rate.
guide.relatedDebtToIncome: the share of your income that goes on all your credit payments.
guide.relatedEarlyRepayment: what a lump-sum repayment saves, and how much it lowers the payment.
guide.exampleSetup: Say you still owe {{balance}} with {{term}} left. Your loan follows an index at {{index}} plus a spread of {{spread}}, so you pay {{rate}}: {{payment}} a month, and {{interest}} in interest to the end of the loan.
guide.exampleRise: At the next revision the index rises to {{newIndex}}, so your rate becomes {{newRate}}. The payment goes up to {{newPayment}}: {{monthlyChange}} more a month ({{percent}}), {{yearlyChange}} more over the next 12 payments and {{interestChange}} more interest by the end of the loan, if the rate stays there.
guide.exampleStress: A rise of {{stressStep}} points instead, to a rate of {{stressRate}}, would take the payment to {{stressPayment}}, {{stressChange}} more than today.
guide.exampleIncome: On a net income of {{income}} a month, the payment takes {{currentShare}} of it today, {{newShare}} after the first rise and {{stressShare}} after the larger one, which the debt-to-income bands rate as “{{stressBand}}”.
guide.methodIntro: Each payment is the level payment that clears the balance over the months left, from the same fixed-rate engine as the mortgage calculator:

methodItems.change: The monthly change is the first payment at the new rate minus the first payment at today's rate, both on today's balance over the same months.
methodItems.year: The yearly change compares the sum of the first 12 payments in each schedule, or all remaining payments if fewer are left. Payments are rounded individually, so the total can differ from the monthly change multiplied by the number of payments.
methodItems.interest: The change in interest is the interest of the new schedule minus today's, both to the end of the loan.
methodItems.income: The share of income is the payment divided by the net income you enter, read against the debt-to-income calculator's bands: under {{caution}}% healthy, {{caution}}% to {{high}}% caution and above {{high}}% high. They are a rule of thumb, not a lender's limit.
methodItems.privacy: The calculation runs in your browser. The figures you enter stay on your device and are not saved.

assumptions.fromNextMonth: The new rate applies from your next payment to the end of the loan. In practice it is revised again at every reset date, so each result is one scenario, not a forecast.
assumptions.sameTerm: The balance and the time left stay as they are, and the payment is what changes. Some lenders can keep the payment and change the term instead.
assumptions.statement: Today's payment is worked out from the index and spread you enter. Your statement can differ by a few cents, and insurance and account fees are left out.
assumptions.noFeed: You enter the index yourself: the calculator has no index data of its own. Take the current value from your contract, your lender or the body that publishes the index.

guide.limits: The calculator accepts balances from {{minBalance}} to {{maxBalance}}, up to {{maxYears}} years left, an index from {{minIndex}} to {{maxIndex}} and a spread up to {{maxSpread}}.
guide.contractIntro: How a real revision works depends on your contract and on the rules where you live. None of this is built into the calculator:

resetDates.body: How often the rate is revised, which day's index value counts and when the new payment starts.

capsFloors.body: Some contracts limit how far the rate can rise or fall, or stop it going below a set level. The calculator only keeps the rate from going below 0%.

index.body: Euribor, a central bank rate or a national reference rate, each with its own terms (for example 3, 6 or 12 months) and publication schedule.

mixed.body: A fixed period comes first and the variable rate after it. Enter the balance and the time left as they will be when the variable period starts.

guide.contractOutro: Your lender's own figures are the ones that count. Use this calculator to plan ahead of a revision, then check its figures against your lender's.

terms.incomeShare: Payment as a share of income

guide.zeroRate: When the index plus the spread is below 0%, the rate is taken as 0% and the payment is simply the balance divided by the number of payments.

guide.exampleLoan: A car priced at {{price}} with a {{deposit}} deposit leaves {{financedAmount}} to finance. Over {{months}} months at a {{rate}} nominal annual rate, with {{upfrontFees}} in upfront fees and {{monthlyFees}} in monthly fees, the first payment is {{payment}}.
guide.exampleRunning: Set aside {{monthlyFuel}} a month for fuel, plus {{annualInsurance}} a year for insurance, {{annualTax}} for tax and {{annualMaintenance}} for maintenance. Running costs average {{running}} per month, putting the monthly budget during the loan at {{budget}}.
guide.methodLoan: Subtract the deposit from the price. Calculate a level monthly payment on the balance using the nominal annual rate divided by 12, then add the monthly fee. At 0% interest, divide the amount financed by the number of months. The displayed payment is the first one. Later payments can differ slightly because of cent rounding.
guide.methodBudget: Divide the annual insurance, tax and maintenance amounts by 12 and round each monthly reserve to cents. Add fuel and the loan payment to estimate the monthly budget while you repay the loan. Once the loan is paid off, only running costs remain.
guide.methodApr: The estimated APR is the annual rate that discounts the monthly payments and their fees to the amount financed less upfront fees. It is available when that net amount is positive. The lender’s APR may include other costs or payment dates, so use the lender’s disclosures when comparing offers.
guide.source: Your Europe guide to consumer credit and APR
guide.assumptionLoan: The estimate assumes a fixed-rate loan with monthly payments, no balloon payment and no lease. Enter the actual price and financing terms you were quoted for the new or used car. Enter zero for both price and deposit to estimate running costs for a car you already own.
guide.assumptionFees: Upfront financing fees are paid at purchase with the deposit. Enter any financing-related insurance or fees only once. The calculator does not infer taxes or charges from your quote.
guide.assumptionRunning: The monthly budget covers the costs shown. It excludes depreciation, resale value, parking, tolls and unexpected repairs beyond your maintenance reserve. Annual bills can fall due in a single month even though the calculator spreads them across the year.

That is {{total}} in total, which you pay on top of the deposit and should add to your savings target.
guide.methodBase: The tax base is the higher of the purchase price and the patrimonial tax value (VPT).
guide.methodImt: For homes, IMT is the base multiplied by the rate of its band minus a fixed deduction (parcela a abater) that makes the tax progressive. Above the last progressive band the rate applies to the whole value without deduction. Rustic land pays 5% and other urban property or land 6.5%.
guide.methodStamp: Stamp duty is 0.8% of the base on the purchase (verba 1.1) and, if you take a mortgage, 0.6% of the amount borrowed (verba 17.1.4, loans of five years or more).
guide.methodRounding: IMT and each stamp duty are rounded to the cent separately, as the tax authority assesses them. Stamp duty on interest and fees is not included.

guide.assumptionScope: This calculator follows Portuguese tax law and only applies to property located in Portugal, whatever your country of residence. It is educational and not tax advice.

guide.whatTitle: What a personal loan really costs
guide.whatBody1: With a fixed-rate personal loan, you make roughly equal monthly payments over a fixed term. Each payment covers interest on the outstanding balance and repays part of the principal. As the balance falls, less of the payment goes to interest and more goes to principal.
guide.whatBody2: The interest rate is only part of the price. Lenders often add a fee when the loan starts and a monthly charge, such as a collection fee or an insurance premium. Those fees come on top of the interest, and on a small or short loan they can cost more than the interest itself.
guide.whatBody3: Before you borrow, check that the payment fits: next to the credit payments you already make, and inside the budget you already live on.
guide.relatedDebtToIncome: shows what share of your income your credit payments, this one included, would take.
guide.relatedHouseholdBudget: shows where your money goes each month, so you can see what the new payment would have to replace.
guide.aprTitle: The interest rate and the APR are not the same
guide.aprBody1: The interest rate in an offer is a nominal annual rate: it sets each month's interest, a twelfth of it on the balance still owed. It leaves out the fees and, because interest is charged every month, it understates the yearly cost even of a loan with no fees.
guide.aprBody2: The annual percentage rate puts everything into one figure. It is the yearly rate at which the money you actually receive (the amount less the upfront fees) equals every payment you make, fees included. Two offers for the same amount and term can be compared by their APR: the lower one costs less.
guide.aprBody3: Each lender works out its APR under its own country's rules, which can include costs this calculator doesn't ask about and count months differently. The APR shown here is an estimate for comparing offers, not the figure in a contract.
guide.exampleIntro: Say you borrow {{amount}} over {{months}} months at a nominal rate of {{rate}}, with no fees.
guide.exampleNoFees: The monthly payment is {{payment}}. Over the term you pay {{interest}} in interest and {{totalRepaid}} in all. Even with no fees, the APR is {{apr}}, a little above {{rate}}, because interest is charged every month.
guide.exampleFees: Now add {{upfront}} of upfront fees and {{monthlyFee}} a month in fees. You receive {{received}}, and each payment rises to {{paymentWithFees}}. The fees add {{fees}}, so the cost of credit grows to {{cost}} and you pay {{totalRepaidFees}} in all.
guide.exampleApr: The interest rate is still {{rate}}, but the APR rises to {{aprFees}}. That is the figure to compare with another offer: a loan at a higher rate with no fees can cost less.
guide.exampleOutro: The calculator above starts from this loan without the fees, so you can enter your own offer.
guide.methodTitle: How the calculator works it out
guide.methodIntro: The monthly payment is the level payment that repays the amount over the term at the monthly rate, and the APR is the rate that balances what you receive against what you pay:
guide.methodApr: The APR is the rate that solves the last line: what you receive at the start, the amount borrowed less the upfront fees, equals each month's payment plus the monthly fees, discounted by one plus the APR to the power of the month's number divided by 12, each month counting as a twelfth of a year. The calculator finds it by bisection.
guide.methodRounding: Every figure is worked in whole cents. Each payment is worked out again from the balance still owed, so the payments stay within a cent of each other, the last one clears the balance exactly, and the schedule adds up to the totals.
guide.methodPrivacy: The calculation runs in your browser. Nothing you enter is sent or stored.
guide.assumptionFixedRate: The rate is fixed for the whole term, and every payment is made on time.
guide.assumptionFees: The upfront fees are paid, or taken off the amount, when the loan starts; the monthly fees are the same every month.
guide.assumptionOtherCosts: Costs the calculator doesn't ask about, such as optional insurance, late-payment charges or an early repayment fee, are left out.
guide.assumptionLimits: Amounts from {{minAmount}} to {{maxAmount}}, terms from {{minMonths}} to {{maxMonths}} months and rates up to {{maxRate}}.

guide.rulesTitle: Série F rules this calculator follows
guide.rulesIntro: Rules from the Série F ficha técnica on the IGCP website, read in {{rulesDate}} (Portaria n.º 149-A/2023, amended by Despacho n.º 11797/2024 and Despachos n.º 5392/2026 and n.º 5839/2026). Rules can change, and the issuer’s current terms are the ones that count.
guide.ruleTerm: Term of {{termYears}} years. You can redeem, in whole or in part, from the first interest date; the calculator uses whole years held.
guide.ruleRate: Each quarter earns the base rate at the start of that quarter plus the permanence bonus for the subscription year. The base rate is E3, the average of the 3-month Euribor over the previous 10 business days, rounded to three decimals, with no margin added. It is set on the third-to-last business day of each month for the following month, and limited to between 0% and {{maxBase}}.
guide.ruleTax: Interest is paid quarterly and capitalised automatically after IRS, withheld at source at {{irsRate}}.
guide.ruleRedeem: Only individuals can hold certificates. The limit is {{maxAmount}} per savings account in Série F, with a minimum of {{minAmount}}.
guide.sourceSheet: Série F ficha técnica on the IGCP website (read on 20 November 2026)
guide.sourceIgcp: IGCP: Série F interest rate for new subscriptions in {{referenceMonth}} ({{referenceRate}})
guide.exampleText: Subscribe {{amount}} and hold for {{years}} years with a {{baseRate}} base rate. The certificates earn {{grossInterest}} in gross interest, of which {{irs}} goes to IRS, leaving {{netInterest}} net. The balance reaches {{finalValue}}, a net yield of {{netYield}} a year.
guide.methodQuarterBody: Each quarter earns a quarter of the annual rate (base rate plus bonus) on the current balance. Amounts are rounded to the cent each quarter.
guide.methodTaxBody: {{irsRate}} of each quarter’s interest is withheld, and the net interest is added to the balance, so later quarters earn interest on it.
guide.methodYieldBody: The net annual yield is the yearly compound growth from the amount subscribed to the final balance. The gross figures show interest before IRS.
guide.assumptionBase: The base rate is the one you enter and stays fixed for the whole stay. It starts at the rate the IGCP set for {{referenceMonth}} ({{referenceRateNote}}), which it sets again every month, so actual interest will differ. Check the current rate on the IGCP website.
guide.assumptionRules: The IRS rate is the general rate for this kind of income. Your own tax situation, and rule changes after {{rulesDate}}, are not modelled.
guide.assumptionScope: This is general information, not a recommendation to buy or avoid any product, and it does not compare certificates with other savings.

read.title: How to read the index
read.what: Every month banks in Portugal report to Banco de Portugal the interest rate on the new term deposits they took from households. The index is the average of those rates across banks, weighted by the amount of new business: what was actually agreed. The euro-area line is the same statistic for all euro-area banks, for comparison.
read.notBest: It is not the best rate on offer. An average includes small deposits, existing customers and banks that pay little, so a campaign or promotional rate can be well above it, and some deposits earn less.
read.noRecommendation: No bank or product is named or ranked here. Use the average to judge whether an offer looks high or low, then compare current offers yourself, including their conditions.

example.title: Worked example

example.real: With inflation at {{inflation}} a year, the same money loses {{inflationCost}} of purchasing power over the term, so what is left after inflation is {{realGain}}.
example.year: Looking back, in {{year}}, the latest complete year, the average new deposit paid {{yearRate}}; after inflation and the 28% IRS the real rate was {{yearReal}}.

method.title: How it is calculated
method.intro: The rates are published statistics. WonderMoney adds only these calculations:

steps.aBody: The plain average of the twelve monthly averages of the year. It does not weight months by how much was deposited.
steps.bBody: The change in the annual average Portuguese consumer price index from the previous year to the year.
steps.cBody: (1 + rate) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1. For the after-tax figure, 28% IRS is taken off the rate first.
steps.dBody: Simple interest for the term in whole months, paid at maturity, with 28% withheld, at the average rate of the maturity group. What inflation takes is the amount × ((1 + inflation)^(months ÷ 12) − 1).

method.realRate: Dividing rather than subtracting matters when rates are high: it measures how much more the money can buy, not just the gap between two percentages.

Retrieved on {{retrieved}}.

data.reuse: The ECB allows free use of its statistics when they are reproduced accurately and the source is cited. This page republishes monthly values and loads no data at runtime: the numbers change only when the data file is refreshed.

items.average: An average of new business: it mixes deposit sizes, banks and customers. Your rate may be higher or lower.
items.lag: The statistics are published monthly with a delay, and the latest month can be revised.
items.tax: Tax: 28% is the IRS withholding rate on interest for residents. Your situation can differ, for example if you include the interest in your annual tax return.
items.inflation: Inflation: your own prices differ from the national average, and future inflation is unknown. The calculator holds the rate you enter for the whole term.
items.buckets: Maturity groups with no new deposits in a month show n/a. For a term in such a group the calculator uses the all-maturities average.

method.title: How it is calculated
method.intro: Each figure comes from the same engine as the term deposit calculator:

steps.aBody: Amount × TANB × term in months ÷ 12, paid in one payment at maturity.

guide.example: On a gross salary of {{gross}} a month, unmarried with no dependants, in mainland Portugal and with a cash meal allowance of {{meal}} a month, IRS withholding is {{withholding}} and Social Security is {{socialSecurity}}. With the holiday and Christmas allowances paid separately, a regular month nets {{net}}, each allowance payment nets {{allowanceNet}} and the year nets {{annual}}.
guide.methodWithholding: IRS withholding follows the 2026 monthly tables: the monthly pay times the marginal rate of its row, minus the row's parcela a abater and a fixed amount for each dependant. From three dependants the rate drops by one percentage point.
guide.methodSocialSecurity: Employee Social Security is 11% of the taxable pay, including meal allowance above the exempt limit.
guide.methodMeal: The meal allowance is exempt up to the daily limit, which depends on whether it is paid in cash or on a meal card. The calculator adds only the excess to the taxable pay.
guide.methodAllowances: With 14 payments, the holiday and Christmas allowances are each taxed on their own, as the tables require. In twelfths, the extra pay is added to each month.
guide.methodBudget: The net figures are what reaches your account, so they are the right starting point for a monthly budget.
guide.finalTitle: Withholding is not your final IRS
guide.final: The amount withheld each month is an advance payment. The Tax Authority settles your real IRS in the annual return, using your whole year's income and your deductions. Withholding can be higher or lower than the tax you finally owe, which is why many people get a refund or a payment due.
guide.unsupportedYouth: IRS Jovem (the young worker regime) is not applied.
guide.unsupportedDisability: The tables for people with a disability, and the pension tables, are not included.
guide.unsupportedNovember: The one-off adjustment for income paid in November 2026 (Despacho 12523-A/2026, mainland) is ignored. It halves the withholding for that month only.
guide.unsupportedOther: Other income, overtime, non-residents, voluntary higher withholding rates and employer costs are outside this estimate.

guide.howFormula: Find the row that holds the monthly pay, multiply the pay by the marginal rate and subtract the parcela a abater. Subtract the extra amount for each dependant, and the result is the withholding.
guide.howTransition: In the first rows the parcela a abater is a formula with the letter R, which is the monthly pay. It makes the withholding rise gently from zero, so a small raise never lowers net pay.
guide.howDependants: Each dependant lowers the withholding by a fixed amount. With three or more dependants, the marginal rate of the row is one percentage point lower.
guide.howTables: Table I serves unmarried people without dependants and married people with two earners. Table II serves unmarried people with dependants and table III married people with one earner.
guide.finalTitle: Withholding is not the final tax
guide.final: The tables set how much your employer withholds each month. They do not calculate your final IRS, which the annual return settles with the brackets above, your whole income and your deductions.

guide.unsupportedYouth: IRS Jovem, which has its own rules.
guide.unsupportedNovember: The one-off adjustment for income paid in November 2026 on the mainland, which halves the withholding for that month only.
